Lesson 5.1

5.1 What an anomaly (unusual activity) is

Slides 6–21≈ 30 min

In Topic 3 you built a reference database — the baseline — of what the Atelier Nordik network does when nothing is wrong. In Topic 4 you learned to read the three sources of monitoring data: event logs, network traffic and network files or system activity. Lesson 5.1 answers the question that every monitoring job comes down to: what exactly is an "anomaly", how does a monitoring tool decide that something is unusual, and why is "unusual" not the same word as "dangerous"? The lesson is deliberately precise, because the vocabulary you fix today is the vocabulary of every alert you will triage in lesson 5.2 and of every finding you will write in Lab 3.

5.1.1 Four words that must stay separate: event, log record, baseline, anomaly

An event is a single observable occurrence on a system or a network: one user logs on, one TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connection is opened, one file is written, one packet crosses the firewall. An event has no opinion attached to it; it simply happened.

A log record (or log entry) is the written trace of an event, produced by the system that saw it: one line of auth.log, one Windows Security event 4625, one firewall log line, one row of a flow export. A record carries the fields you studied in Class 14 — timestamp, source, destination, account, outcome — and it is the raw material of everything that follows. One event can produce several records (the firewall and the server both see the same connection) and some events produce none (nobody logs what nobody collects — the coverage problem of Topic 6).

The baseline is the statistical description of the events that occur when the network is operating normally: how many logons per hour, which hosts talk to which, how much traffic leaves each workstation, which services run at which times. In Lab 2 you computed it from two weeks of collection (September 21 to October 4). A baseline is always attached to a scope (which host, which metric) and a context (which hour of the day, which day of the week), because "normal" at 10:00 on a Tuesday is not "normal" at 03:00 on a Sunday.

An anomaly is an observation that deviates from the baseline by more than an agreed tolerance. That sentence contains the three parts of every anomaly definition: a reference (the baseline), a measure of deviation (how far the observation is from the reference) and a threshold (how far is too far). Remove any of the three and the word "anomaly" has no meaning: without a baseline there is nothing to deviate from, without a measure you cannot compare, and without a threshold every observation is either always or never an anomaly.

The course outline calls an anomaly an unusual activity. Keep that phrase in mind, because it says nothing about intent. Unusual activity has a cause; the cause may be an attacker, a failure, a change made by the IT (Information Technology) contractor, a new employee, or a holiday. Finding the cause is diagnosis (lesson 5.4); today we only learn to recognise and name the deviation.

5.1.2 Unusual is not malicious: anomaly, incident, attack, false alarm

Four more words, again to be kept apart. An anomaly is a measured deviation. A security incident is an anomaly whose cause is an actual or imminent violation of the organisation's security policy — the confidentiality, integrity or availability of information or systems (the CIA (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) triad of Topic 1). An attack is a deliberate attempt by a person or a program to cause such a violation; an incident may also be caused by error or failure without any attacker. A false alarm is an anomaly that, once examined, turns out to have a harmless explanation.

The relationship between these words is one of inclusion: every incident starts as an anomaly, but most anomalies are not incidents. On a network of fourteen people, a week of monitoring produces dozens of deviations; experience in small organisations shows that the large majority are explained by maintenance, updates, backups, new software, holidays and human mistakes. This is not a reason to ignore anomalies — the few real incidents hide among them — but it is the reason why lesson 5.2 exists: the anomalies have to be sorted before anyone can analyse them.

Two further terms describe the evidence that connects an anomaly to a possible incident. A precursor is a sign that an incident may occur in the future (a port scan is the classic precursor: the attacker is mapping before acting). An indicator is a sign that an incident may have occurred or may be occurring now (a successful logon from an address that has just produced twenty failures). Indicators that are specific enough to be shared and searched for — a file hash, a domain name, an IP (Internet Protocol) address, a pattern of commands — are called IoC (Indicator of Compromise). The Professor Messer video listed below walks through the common ones: unexpected account lockouts, concurrent sessions, impossible travel, unusual resource consumption, logs that go missing.

5.1.3 Three families of anomalies: point, contextual, collective

Anomaly-detection research classifies anomalies into three families, and the classification is practical because each family is caught by a different test. Figure 5.1-A shows the three on one baseline.

  • Point anomaly. A single observation is far outside the band of normal values, whatever the context. Example: WS-10-44 normally opens about 60 outbound connections in its busiest hour; one hour shows 112. Another example: a 1.2 GB file transfer from a server that never sends more than 50 MB. The test is a distance test: how far is this value from the mean?
  • Contextual anomaly. The value itself is ordinary, but it occurs in a context in which it is not expected. Example: 47 outbound connections is an ordinary workday hour for WS-10-44; at 19:00 on a Thursday, when the workstation is normally idle and the designer has left, it is unusual. Another example: a VPN (Virtual Private Network) logon by the backup account, which never uses VPN (Virtual Private Network). The test is a conditional test: is this value normal given the hour, the day, the account, the host?
  • Collective anomaly. Each observation, taken alone, is ordinary; the set or sequence of observations is not. Example: one failed logon is daily life; twenty-three failed logons in four minutes on seven different account names is a password-guessing attempt. Another example: connections to sixteen different ports of the same server within forty-two seconds — no single connection is suspicious, the pattern is. The test is a pattern test over a window of time: how many, how fast, in what order?

A single episode can belong to several families at once. The Thursday-evening activity of WS-10-44 is contextual (activity in an idle hour), collective (two consecutive unusual hours) and, inside the hour, made of a port-scan sequence. When you write a finding in Lab 3, name the family that your detection rule actually tested, because that is what you can prove.

5.1.4 Where anomalies show up: the three data sources of Topic 4

Every anomaly is observed in one of the three sources you learned to read in Topic 4. The table below gives, for each source, a baseline metric from Lab 2, a normal value for Atelier Nordik and an anomaly of each family. The table is downloadable (Table 5.1-2) and is reused in the Lab 3 instructions.

Notice that the same cause often appears in two sources at once: the SSH (Secure Shell) guessing of Class 14 is 23 records in auth.log (event logs) and 23 short connections in the firewall log (network traffic). Seeing the same anomaly from two independent sources is called corroboration; it raises the confidence that the anomaly is real, which is exactly what the triage score of lesson 5.2 rewards.

5.1.5 How a detector decides that something is unusual

A detector is the rule, program or tool component that turns records into a decision ("unusual" or "normal"). NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-94, the guide to IDS (Intrusion Detection System) and IPS (Intrusion Prevention System), distinguishes three methods; practice adds two more. All five are summarised in Table 5.1-3.

  1. Signature-based detection. The detector compares each record with a list of known bad patterns (a signature): a byte sequence in a packet, a file hash, a command line, a domain name. It is precise for known threats and blind to new ones. Strictly speaking it is not anomaly detection — it does not use a baseline — but it is the first thing a monitoring tool does, and a signature match is also an anomaly in the plain sense: it should not be there.
  2. Threshold-based detection. The detector counts records that satisfy a condition inside a time window and compares the count with a fixed number: "10 or more failed logons within 10 minutes", "10 or more distinct destination ports of one host within 60 seconds". Both Class 14 scripts are threshold detectors. The threshold is chosen by a person, from the baseline and from policy; it is simple, transparent and easy to tune.
  3. Statistical detection. The detector computes, from the baseline, the mean (the average value) and the standard deviation (the typical spread around the average, written σ) of a metric, then measures how many standard deviations the current observation is from the mean. That number is the z-score: z = (observed − mean) / σ. A common tolerance is |z| ≥ 3: for a metric whose values are roughly bell-shaped, fewer than 0.3 % of normal observations fall that far from the mean, so a value beyond three standard deviations is far more likely to be an anomaly than noise. Example 5.1 is a statistical detector.
  4. Behavioural (profile-based) detection. The baseline is kept per entity — per user, per host, per service — and per context (hour, weekday). The detector then asks the contextual question: is this value normal for this host at this hour? Commercial products call this UEBA (User and Entity Behaviour Analytics). Example 5.1 is also behavioural, because its baseline is one host's profile by hour of the day.
  5. Machine-learning detection. A model learns the shape of normal activity from many variables at once and scores new observations by how badly they fit. It can find combinations no human would write a rule for, at the price of being harder to explain. It is mentioned here so that you recognise the term in product documentation; it is not used in this course.

Two practical rules follow. First, a statistical test needs a sensible baseline: computing a mean and a standard deviation from three days of data, or from a period that contained an incident, produces a tolerance band that is either too narrow (constant false alarms) or too wide (misses). Second, a z-score alone over-reacts when the baseline is tiny: when the mean is 2 and σ is 1.2, an observation of 6 has z = 3.3 and would be flagged, although four extra connections at night mean nothing. Example 5.1 therefore adds a second condition, a minimum absolute difference, before flagging an hour. Good detectors combine conditions; a single number rarely suffices.

5.1.6 The four outcomes of a detector

Whatever its method, a detector can only be right or wrong in two directions, which gives four outcomes (Table 5.1-4).

  • TP (True Positive) — the detector flags an observation, and the observation really is unwanted. The SSH (Secure Shell) guessing from 203.0.113.57 flagged by the 10-in-10-minutes rule.
  • FP (False Positive) — the detector flags an observation that is in fact harmless. The Patch-Wednesday hour flagged as a point anomaly in Example 5.1: the rule worked as designed, but the cause is the IT (Information Technology) contractor's update push. Some teams call this particular case a benign true positive — the rule correctly detected real activity that happens to be authorised — and keep the words "false positive" for rules that fired on nothing at all (a parsing error, a wrong threshold). Lesson 5.2 uses both words and explains which to write in the ticket.
  • FN (False Negative) — unwanted activity occurred and the detector did not flag it. The six outbound SYN (synchronize flag of a TCP segment) packets to port 4444 would be a false negative for a rule that only counts replies; the only way to discover a false negative is a second, independent detector or a later investigation.
  • TN (True Negative) — nothing unwanted happened and nothing was flagged. The silent majority of records.

Two consequences matter for monitoring. The base-rate effect: on a network producing 10,000 records a day, a rule with a false-positive rate of only 1 % still produces about 100 false alarms a day, far more than the handful of real incidents, so even a very good rule needs triage behind it. And the trade-off: lowering a threshold catches more true positives and produces more false positives at the same time; raising it does the reverse. Choosing the threshold is a decision about which error the organisation prefers, and it is revisited in Topic 6.4 ("fewer false alarms").

5.1.7 Benign causes, and the difference with a performance anomaly

Before leaving the lesson, list the causes of anomalies that are not incidents, because a technician who recognises them saves hours. Scheduled jobs (backups, update pushes, antivirus definition downloads, report generation at month end), changes (new software, a new employee, a new printer, a firewall rule added by the contractor), calendar effects (holidays — Thanksgiving is Monday —, the switch from daylight-saving time on November 1, which shifts every "hour of the day" baseline by one hour), failures (a disk filling up, a certificate expiring, a service restarting in a loop), and people (a user working late before a deadline, a typing error repeated three times). The maintenance calendar and the allow-list of lesson 5.2 exist to document these causes before the alert arrives.

Finally, recall Topic 1.5: a performance anomaly (slow server, saturated link, full disk) and a security anomaly (unauthorised access, data leaving the network) are detected by the same monitoring and often look alike at first — a denial-of-service attack and a popular new web page both raise the request rate. The distinction is made in diagnosis, not in detection; what detection must guarantee is that both reach a human. Alert A-01 of Example 5.2 (the log disk at 86 %) is a performance anomaly with a security consequence: if the disk fills, the monitoring server stops recording and every later detection becomes a false negative.

Example 5.1 — The designer workstation that woke up at night

Task of the example. Compare four observed days of one host (WS-10-44, outbound TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connection attempts per hour, Tuesday October 6 to Friday October 9) with the hourly baseline built in Lab 2, flag the hours that deviate beyond the tolerance, and name the family of each flagged hour.

Relation to the lesson. The example applies, in order, every element of 5.1.1 (reference, deviation, threshold), uses the statistical and behavioural methods of 5.1.5 (z-score on a per-host, per-hour profile), produces the three families of 5.1.3, and ends with one true positive, one benign flag and one near miss — the four outcomes of 5.1.6.

Lab 3 deliverable. The output file anomalies.csv and the chart below are the "detect" input of Lab 3, Part 3 of the Integrative Project; the baseline and the observed week are the files you will reuse.

The monitoring server MON-250 receives the LAN (Local Area Network) mirror port and the OPNsense firewall log. In Lab 2 you configured it to count, for each workstation, the number of outbound TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connection attempts per hour, and you stored two weeks of counts as the baseline: for every hour of the day, the mean and the standard deviation of the count on workdays. For WS-10-44 the profile is what you expect of a designer's workstation: almost nothing between 20:00 and 07:00 (two or three automatic connections an hour — time synchronisation, antivirus check-ins), a ramp at 07:00–08:00, about sixty connections an hour during work, a dip at lunch, and a drop after 17:00.

On Saturday morning you load the four workdays of the week (96 hourly values) and run baseline_deviation.py. The script computes the z-score of each hour, applies the two conditions (|z| ≥ 3 and a difference of at least 10 connections), then looks for runs of consecutive flagged hours. It flags three hours: Wednesday 14:00 (112 connections, z = 3.27, a point anomaly — the hour of the Patch-Wednesday update push, a benign cause documented in the maintenance calendar), Thursday 19:00 (47 connections, z = 29.3, contextual: activity in an idle hour) and Thursday 20:00 (14 connections, z = 9.2, contextual), the last two forming a collective run. It does not flag Friday 10:00 (98 connections, z = 2.13: elevated but inside the tolerance) nor Tuesday 03:00 (6 connections, z = 3.3 but only four connections above the mean: the absolute-difference guard applies).

The Thursday-evening run is the hour in which, in Class 14, you saw WS-10-44 probe sixteen ports of srv-web01 and send six unanswered SYN (synchronize flag of a TCP segment) packets to 198.51.100.200:4444. Two independent detectors — the traffic rule of Class 14 and the baseline rule of today — now point at the same host and the same hour: the anomaly is corroborated. What the process on WS-10-44 was, and whether the designer was present, remain open questions for Lab 3.

The code that illustrates the example — baseline_deviation.py

What the script does. baseline_deviation.py reads baseline_hourly.csv (24 rows: hour, mean, standard deviation) and observed_week.csv (96 rows: hour, count), computes the z-score of every observed hour against the baseline of the same hour of the day, flags the hours that pass both conditions, classifies them (point or contextual, plus collective for runs), writes anomalies.csv and prints the flagged hours.

Relation to the lecture. Lines 1–30 define the three parts of the anomaly definition (reference file, tolerance Z_THRESHOLD, guard MIN_ABS_DIFF); z_score() is the statistical method of 5.1.5; evaluate() produces the point/contextual families of 5.1.3; mark_collective() produces the collective family; the printed summary is what you will paste into the Lab 3 report. The simulator below runs the same algorithm in the page, hour by hour, so that it can be paused and discussed.

baseline_deviation.py — a comment line before every line of code
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# ============================================================================
# baseline_deviation.py — Class 15, Example 5.1 (Atelier Nordik inc., fictional)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# TASK: compare one host's hourly activity (outbound TCP connection attempts of
# the workstation WS-10-44) with the hourly baseline built in Lab 2, compute how
# far each observed hour deviates from "normal" (the z-score), flag the hours
# that deviate beyond the tolerance, and classify each flagged hour as a point,
# contextual or collective anomaly. The result file (anomalies.csv) is the
# "detect" input of Lab 3 — Part 3 of the Integrative Project.
# RELATION TO THE LECTURE: lesson 5.1 defines an anomaly as an observation that
# deviates from the baseline beyond a tolerance; this script is that definition
# written as code (baseline + tolerance + deviation + classification).
# Educational material — Cyber.SoHo / Asen Grozdanov — (c) 2026 Cyber.SoHo.
# Use only in an authorized lab environment (Legal Notice v2.0, section 7.2).
# ============================================================================

# The csv module reads and writes comma-separated files; both inputs and the output are CSV.
import csv
# The math module gives us sqrt and fabs; we use fabs for the absolute value of z.
import math
# The datetime module parses the "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM" text of each observed hour into a date object.
from datetime import datetime

# File that holds the baseline: one row per hour of the day (0-23) with the mean and standard deviation.
BASELINE_FILE = "baseline_hourly.csv"
# File that holds the observations to test: one row per hour of the observed week.
OBSERVED_FILE = "observed_week.csv"
# File that will receive the result: every observed hour with its z-score, flag and classification.
OUTPUT_FILE = "anomalies.csv"
# Tolerance expressed in standard deviations: an hour is "unusual" when |z| >= 3 (the classic 3-sigma rule).
Z_THRESHOLD = 3.0
# Guard against tiny baselines: the observed value must also differ from the mean by at least this many connections.
MIN_ABS_DIFF = 10
# A "normally quiet" hour is one whose baseline mean is below this value (used to detect contextual anomalies).
QUIET_MEAN = 5
# Activity level that is clearly real work and not background noise in a quiet hour.
QUIET_ACTIVITY = 10


# This function reads the baseline file and returns a dictionary {hour: (mean, stdev)}.
def load_baseline(path):
    # Start with an empty dictionary that will be filled hour by hour.
    baseline = {}
    # Open the CSV file for reading; "newline=''" is the documented way to open CSV files in Python.
    with open(path, newline="") as f:
        # DictReader returns each row as a dictionary keyed by the column names of the header line.
        for row in csv.DictReader(f):
            # Convert the hour text ("19") to an integer so it can be used as a key.
            hour = int(row["hour"])
            # Store the mean and the standard deviation as floating-point numbers.
            baseline[hour] = (float(row["mean_connections"]), float(row["stdev_connections"]))
    # Give the completed dictionary back to the caller.
    return baseline


# This function reads the observed file and returns a list of (datetime, count) pairs in time order.
def load_observed(path):
    # Start with an empty list.
    observed = []
    # Open the observations file.
    with open(path, newline="") as f:
        # Read it row by row as dictionaries.
        for row in csv.DictReader(f):
            # Parse the text "2026-10-08 19:00" into a datetime object.
            when = datetime.strptime(row["hour_start"], "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M")
            # Add the pair (time, number of connection attempts) to the list.
            observed.append((when, int(row["connection_attempts"])))
    # Return the list sorted by time, so the collective-anomaly test can look at consecutive hours.
    return sorted(observed)


# This function computes the z-score: how many standard deviations the value is away from the mean.
def z_score(value, mean, stdev):
    # A standard deviation of zero would divide by zero; we use a small floor so the formula stays defined.
    safe_stdev = stdev if stdev > 0 else 0.5
    # z = (observed - mean) / standard deviation; positive means "more than usual", negative "less than usual".
    return (value - mean) / safe_stdev


# This function decides whether one observed hour is flagged, and why.
def evaluate(when, value, mean, stdev):
    # Compute the deviation in standard deviations.
    z = z_score(value, mean, stdev)
    # Compute the plain difference in connections, used by the absolute-difference guard.
    diff = value - mean
    # Flag the hour only when BOTH conditions hold: the z-score is beyond the tolerance AND the difference is material.
    flagged = math.fabs(z) >= Z_THRESHOLD and math.fabs(diff) >= MIN_ABS_DIFF
    # Default classification text when nothing is flagged.
    kind = "normal"
    # Default explanatory note.
    note = "within tolerance"
    # If the hour is flagged, choose the anomaly family (contextual or point); "collective" is added later.
    if flagged:
        # A quiet hour (baseline mean below QUIET_MEAN) that shows real activity is a CONTEXTUAL anomaly: normal value, abnormal time.
        if mean < QUIET_MEAN and value >= QUIET_ACTIVITY:
            # Record the family.
            kind = "contextual"
            # Record the reason in plain words for the report.
            note = "activity during a normally idle hour"
        # Otherwise the value itself is far outside the band of a busy hour: a POINT anomaly.
        else:
            # Record the family.
            kind = "point"
            # Record the reason.
            note = "volume far outside the baseline band"
    # When the z-score is high but the absolute difference is tiny, say so: the guard prevented a noisy flag.
    elif math.fabs(z) >= Z_THRESHOLD:
        # Keep the classification "normal" but explain that the guard applied.
        note = "high z but small absolute difference (guard applied)"
    # Give back everything the report needs for this hour.
    return z, flagged, kind, note


# This function marks runs of two or more consecutive flagged hours as COLLECTIVE anomalies.
def mark_collective(results):
    # Walk through the list by index so we can look at the previous and the next entries.
    for i in range(len(results)):
        # Skip hours that are not flagged.
        if not results[i]["flagged"]:
            # Nothing to do for a normal hour.
            continue
        # Check whether the previous hour is flagged (and exists).
        prev_flagged = i > 0 and results[i - 1]["flagged"]
        # Check whether the next hour is flagged (and exists).
        next_flagged = i + 1 < len(results) and results[i + 1]["flagged"]
        # Two or more consecutive flagged hours form a sustained, collective pattern.
        if prev_flagged or next_flagged:
            # Append the collective family to the classification (an hour can be point + collective).
            results[i]["kind"] = results[i]["kind"] + "+collective"
            # Extend the note so the report says why.
            results[i]["note"] = results[i]["note"] + "; part of a sustained run"
    # Return the updated list.
    return results


# The main routine ties everything together: load, evaluate, classify, write, summarise.
def main():
    # Load the hourly baseline built in Lab 2.
    baseline = load_baseline(BASELINE_FILE)
    # Load the hours to test.
    observed = load_observed(OBSERVED_FILE)
    # Prepare the list that will hold one result dictionary per observed hour.
    results = []
    # Examine every observed hour in time order.
    for when, value in observed:
        # Fetch the baseline mean and standard deviation for this hour of the day.
        mean, stdev = baseline[when.hour]
        # Evaluate the hour against the baseline.
        z, flagged, kind, note = evaluate(when, value, mean, stdev)
        # Store the result as a dictionary so the columns are named.
        results.append({"hour_start": when.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M"), "observed": value,
                        "baseline_mean": mean, "baseline_stdev": stdev, "z": round(z, 2),
                        "flagged": flagged, "kind": kind, "note": note})
    # Add the collective classification to runs of flagged hours.
    results = mark_collective(results)
    # Open the output file for writing.
    with open(OUTPUT_FILE, "w", newline="") as f:
        # Create a writer that uses the dictionary keys as column names.
        writer = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=list(results[0].keys()))
        # Write the header line.
        writer.writeheader()
        # Write every result row.
        writer.writerows(results)
    # Count the flagged hours for the summary.
    flagged_hours = [r for r in results if r["flagged"]]
    # Print a summary line: how many hours were tested and how many were flagged.
    print(f"Tested {len(results)} hours; flagged {len(flagged_hours)} -> {OUTPUT_FILE}")
    # Print one line per flagged hour so the technician sees the detections immediately.
    for r in flagged_hours:
        # Show the time, the value, the baseline and the classification.
        print(f"  {r['hour_start']}  observed={r['observed']:>4}  baseline={r['baseline_mean']:>5}±{r['baseline_stdev']:<4}  z={r['z']:>6}  {r['kind']}: {r['note']}")


# Standard Python idiom: run main() only when the file is executed directly, not when it is imported.
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Start the program.
    main()
▶ Simulator 5.1 — the script, hour by hour (same algorithm, same data)

Grey band: baseline mean ± 3 σ for the hour of the day · blue: observed hours as they are tested · rust: flagged hours · amber ring: high z but guard applied. The status line under the chart shows the current hour's computation.

Press Start. Each step tests one hour: it fetches the baseline of that hour of the day, computes z, applies the two conditions and classifies.
Execution log (every step; pause to discuss)
Step-by-step explanation of the script
  1. Imports and constants. The script needs only the standard library (csv, math, datetime). The constants are the policy: tolerance 3 σ, minimum difference 10 connections, a quiet hour is one whose mean is below 5, and an activity of 10 or more in such an hour counts as real activity.
  2. Loading the baseline. load_baseline() builds a dictionary keyed by hour of the day (0–23). Each value is the pair (mean, standard deviation) computed in Lab 2. The dictionary is the reference of the definition.
  3. Loading the observations. load_observed() converts the text time of each row into a real date object and sorts the rows, because the collective test later compares consecutive hours.
  4. The deviation. z_score() divides the difference between the observed value and the mean by the standard deviation. A floor of 0.5 protects against a standard deviation of zero (a metric that never varied during the baseline).
  5. The decision for one hour. evaluate() applies the two conditions. If both hold, it names the family: contextual when the baseline mean is below 5 and the value is 10 or more (activity in an idle hour), point otherwise. When only the z condition holds, it writes a note so that the technician sees why the guard applied.
  6. The collective pass. mark_collective() walks the ordered results and, whenever a flagged hour has a flagged neighbour, appends "+collective" to its family. This is the pattern test of 5.1.3 implemented on the simplest pattern: a run.
  7. Output. main() writes every hour (not only the flagged ones) to anomalies.csv so that the file is a complete record, then prints the flagged hours with their z-scores. Run it with python3 baseline_deviation.py in the folder that contains the two input files.
Expected output of the script:
Tested 96 hours; flagged 3 -> anomalies.csv
  2026-10-07 14:00  observed= 112  baseline= 63.0±15.0  z=  3.27  point: volume far outside the baseline band
  2026-10-08 19:00  observed=  47  baseline=  3.0±1.5   z= 29.33  contextual+collective: activity during a normally idle hour; part of a sustained run
  2026-10-08 20:00  observed=  14  baseline=  2.0±1.3   z=  9.23  contextual+collective: activity during a normally idle hour; part of a sustained run
Flash cards — lesson 5.1
Click a card to reveal the answer on its back; click again to return.
Card 1
What are the three parts of every anomaly definition?
click to reveal
Answer 1
A reference (the baseline), a measure of deviation (for example the z-score) and a threshold (the tolerance). Remove one and "anomaly" has no meaning.
Card 2
Point, contextual, collective — which family is "23 failed logons in 4 minutes"?
click to reveal
Answer 2
Collective: each failed logon is ordinary; the set in a short window is not. The test is a pattern test over a time window.
Card 3
How is the z-score computed and what is the usual tolerance?
click to reveal
Answer 3
z = (observed − mean) / standard deviation, using the baseline of the same context (hour of day). |z| ≥ 3 is the common tolerance; Example 5.1 adds a minimum absolute difference of 10.
Card 4
What is the difference between a precursor and an indicator?
click to reveal
Answer 4
A precursor is a sign that an incident may occur (a port scan); an indicator is a sign that an incident may have occurred or is occurring (a success after many failures). Shareable, specific indicators are IoC (Indicator of Compromise).
Card 5
Why is a flagged Patch-Wednesday hour a problem for the monitoring team even though nothing bad happened?
click to reveal
Answer 5
It is a false positive (or benign true positive): it consumes analysis time. With 10,000 records a day, even a 1 % false-positive rate is about 100 alerts a day — the base-rate effect — so the baseline or the rule must be tuned (Topic 6).
Check-in questions — lesson 5.1
Four multiple-choice questions (one answer each) and two multiple-select questions (the number of expected answers is written in round brackets). Use Hint for a clue, Check to grade your selection, Reveal to see the expected answer and the explanation of every option.
MCQ (Multiple-Choice Question)Question 1


A monitoring tool reports that SRV-AD01 recorded 15 failed logons on the account "administrator" within two minutes. Taken as a whole, this observation is best described as which family of anomaly?
  • Wrong: the number is large only because events were counted over a window; the individual observations are ordinary.
  • Correct: the detection is a count in a 10-minute window — a pattern over a set of ordinary events, which is the definition of a collective anomaly.
  • Wrong: the privileged account raises the impact in triage, but the detection test here is a window count, not a context check.
  • Wrong: three failures by a user who mistypes are normal; fifteen in two minutes on the administrator account are not.
Hint: Ask which test caught it: a distance test on one value, a conditional test on the context, or a pattern test over a window.


MCQ (Multiple-Choice Question)Question 2


The hourly baseline of WS-10-44 at 19:00 is a mean of 3 connections with a standard deviation of 1.5. An observed value of 47 gives which z-score?
  • Wrong: 2.1 is the z-score of the Friday 10:00 value (98 against 66 ± 15).
  • Wrong: dividing by 3 (the mean) instead of 1.5 (the standard deviation) gives about 15; the divisor is σ.
  • Correct: (47 − 3) / 1.5 = 29.3 — far beyond the tolerance of 3.
  • Wrong: 44 is the difference (47 − 3), not the number of standard deviations.
Hint: z = (observed − mean) ÷ standard deviation.


MCQ (Multiple-Choice Question)Question 3


Which statement about a false negative is correct?
  • Wrong: that is a false positive.
  • Correct: the detector missed real activity; by definition the tool itself cannot report it.
  • Wrong: that is a true negative.
  • Wrong: closing an alert is a triage decision (5.2), not a detection outcome.
Hint: Negative = the detector said "nothing"; false = the detector was wrong.


MCQ (Multiple-Choice Question)Question 4


Why does Example 5.1 require a minimum absolute difference of 10 connections in addition to |z| ≥ 3?
  • Wrong: z can be computed for any value; the problem is interpretation, not computation.
  • Correct: a z-score divides by a small σ, so a few extra night-time connections look extreme; the guard keeps the rule from reacting to noise.
  • Wrong: the guard concerns small baselines; the Friday 10:00 value (z = 2.13) shows that 3 is not too high for workday hours.
  • Wrong: there is no such logging behaviour; the guard is a policy choice in the rule.
Hint: Look at the Tuesday 03:00 value in the example: 6 connections, z = 3.3, not flagged.


MSQ (Multiple-Select Question)Question 5


Which of the following are benign (non-incident) causes of anomalies that the monitoring team should document before an alert arrives? (select 3)
  • Correct: a scheduled, documented change — it belongs in the maintenance calendar.
  • Correct: a scheduled job — it belongs in the maintenance calendar and the allow-list.
  • Wrong: this is the password-guessing pattern of Class 14, a precursor or an attack, never benign.
  • Wrong: unexplained outbound contact on an unusual port is exactly what monitoring exists to catch.
  • Correct: a calendar effect that produces contextual anomalies on every host at once unless the baseline is shifted.
  • Wrong: a success following a burst of failures is an indicator, not a benign cause.
Hint: Scheduled jobs, planned changes and calendar effects are benign; patterns of guessing and unexplained outbound contact are not.


MSQ (Multiple-Select Question)Question 6


Which statements about detection methods are correct? (select 3)
  • Correct: that is the definition in NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-94 — precise for known threats, blind to unknown ones.
  • Wrong: a threshold detector compares a count with a fixed number chosen by a person; it does not compute σ.
  • Correct: z = (observed − mean) / σ is the statistical method of 5.1.5.
  • Correct: that is what makes a detector able to find contextual anomalies.
  • Wrong: both Class 14 scripts are threshold detectors (counts in a time window).
  • Wrong: 2.1 is below 3; the Friday 10:00 value of Example 5.1 was elevated but not flagged.
Hint: Match each method with what it compares the record against: a list, a fixed number, a distribution, a profile, a model.


Lesson 5.2
5.2 Reviewing and sorting alerts (triage)
Slides 22–36≈ 30 min


Lesson 5.1 ended with a fact that every monitoring team lives with: detectors produce far more alerts than there are incidents. On Saturday afternoon the technician of Atelier Nordik opens the console of MON-250 and finds twelve alerts waiting from the weekend. Lesson 5.2 teaches the method that decides, in a few minutes per alert and in a repeatable way, what each alert is, how urgent it is, and what happens to it next. That method is triage. It is the first step of the analysis chain — triage (5.2), analysis (5.3), diagnosis and documentation (5.4), communication (5.5) — and it is the step that protects the three later ones from being wasted on noise.





5.2.1 From anomaly to alert: what an alert is, and what it is not


An alert is a message produced by a detector when its condition is met: "rule X matched record Y at time Z". It contains, at minimum, the name of the rule, the time, the source of the data, the asset and, when they exist, the account and the addresses concerned. Most tools also attach a severity chosen by whoever wrote the rule, and a copy of, or a pointer to, the records that triggered it.


The essential point is that an alert is a claim, not a fact. The detector claims that something unusual happened; it has no knowledge of the maintenance calendar, of the fact that the designer works from home on Saturdays, or of the vendor contract that explains a large download. The alert must be verified before it becomes an incident, and the verification has two stages: a short one (triage, this lesson) that decides whether and how fast the alert deserves attention, and a long one (analysis, lesson 5.3) that establishes what actually happened. Figure 5.2-A places triage in that chain: events enter on the left, decisions leave on the right, and a feedback path returns to the rules and the baseline (Topic 6) whenever triage shows that a rule fires for nothing.


Note also what triage is not. It is not the full investigation: an alert that needs a disk image, a packet capture or a conversation with the user is not resolved in triage, it is routed by triage. Teams fix a time box — typically five to fifteen minutes per alert — precisely so that the queue keeps moving.




5.2.2 Triage: the definition and the three verbs


The word comes from emergency medicine, where patients are sorted by urgency before treatment; in security operations it has the same structure. The FIRST (Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams) CSIRT (Computer Security Incident Response Team) Services Framework defines incident triage as the function that categorises, prioritises and produces an initial assessment of a reported event. NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-61 places the same activity inside "detection and analysis" and insists on prioritisation as the most critical decision point of the handling process, because the team cannot work on everything at once. Both sources reduce to three verbs that structure the rest of this lesson:


    

  1. Categorise — say what kind of thing the alert is (an authentication problem, a network reconnaissance, an outbound contact, a data transfer, a health problem of the monitoring itself) and what kind of outcome it is (real, expected, false, duplicate, undetermined).
    2. 

  2. Prioritise — give it a position in the queue, derived from how bad it would be if true (impact) and how likely it is to be true (confidence).
    3. 

  3. Decide and record — choose the next action (escalate, investigate, monitor, close) and write down why, in a form that another person can read on Monday.
    4. 



In a large organisation these verbs are performed by a SOC (Security Operations Center) analyst of the first level, who passes the serious cases to a second level. At Atelier Nordik there is no SOC (Security Operations Center): the technician does the triage, the IT (Information Technology) contractor is the second level, and the owner of the firm is the person to call when an incident record is opened. The method is identical; only the names of the people change.




5.2.3 The five triage questions


Every alert is read with the same five questions. Writing their answers is the "initial assessment" of the definition, and the answers feed directly into the two scales of 5.2.5.


    

  1. What fired? Which rule, on which data source, over which time window, with which threshold. A threshold rule on counts (A-05, A-06) says something different from an informational rule (A-07, A-10) or an absence rule ("no logs for 60 minutes", A-12).
    2. 

  2. Where? Which asset, in which zone, with which criticality from the Lab 1 inventory, and who owns it. The same rule firing on the domain controller and on a designer's workstation does not have the same impact.
    3. 

  3. Who? Which account, with which role. A privileged account (administrator, ops, backup-svc) raises the impact; a service account that never logs on interactively is itself a context.
    4. 

  4. When? At what time, for how long, is it still going on, and does a maintenance window cover it. An attack in progress ranks above an identical pattern that stopped yesterday. The time must be read in one time zone (UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) on the log server, local time in the report), which is why clock drift (A-07) is never irrelevant.
    5. 

  5. How sure are we? What is the evidence: how many records, from how many independent sources, is the address or account in the allow-list, does another alert in the queue concern the same asset (corroboration), could the rule have fired on a parsing error.
    6. 






5.2.4 Categorising the outcome


Besides its kind (authentication, reconnaissance, outbound contact, transfer, health), every alert receives an outcome category at the end of triage. Table 5.2-1 lists the five used in this course.


    

  • True positive — unwanted. The rule fired on activity that is not authorised or not explained. The alert stays open and is prioritised.
    • 

  • Benign true positive — expected. The rule fired correctly on activity that is authorised and documented: a backup, a patch push, a vendor download. The alert is closed with the reference to the document that explains it (calendar entry, allow-list line, contract number). If the same benign alert returns every week, that is a tuning request for Topic 6.4, not a reason to stop reading.
    • 

  • False positive — rule error. The rule fired on nothing: a mis-parsed record, a wrong threshold, a clock problem. Closed, and the rule is sent for correction.
    • 

  • Duplicate. The same cause already produced an open alert (the second occurrence of the port-scan pattern, A-02, is a repetition of Thursday's). Merged into the existing one, which gains a count and a "recurring" mark — recurrence raises confidence, it does not lower it.
    • 

  • Undetermined — needs information. The evidence is insufficient to decide. The alert is kept open with a watch action and a date, never silently closed.
    • 



The distinction between "benign true positive" and "false positive" matters for the feedback loop: in the first case the baseline or the allow-list must be updated (the activity is real and will recur), in the second case the rule is broken. Writing the right one in the ticket is what makes Topic 6 possible.




5.2.5 Severity, impact, confidence, priority


Students regularly confuse two words. Severity is the value the rule writer attached to the rule — "a failed-logon burst is severity 4" — before anything was known about the asset or the context. Priority is the order in which the alerts will be handled, and it is computed during triage from two judgements about this alert on this asset:


Impact (1–5): how bad would it be if the alert is true? NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-61 proposes three components — the functional impact (what the organisation can no longer do), the information impact (what confidentiality or integrity is lost) and the recoverability (how much effort it takes to return to normal). For a small network a practical scale takes the larger of the rule severity and the asset criticality of the Lab 1 inventory, and adds one level when a privileged account is involved (Table 5.2-2). The domain controller at criticality 5 with the administrator account is impact 5 whatever the rule; a workstation at criticality 2 with a severity-3 rule is impact 3.


Confidence (1–5): how likely is it that the alert describes real unwanted activity? Start at 3 ("plausible, unverified"). Add one when an address or account in the alert is neither local nor in the allow-list (an unexplained party). Add one when another open alert concerns the same asset (corroboration — the lesson of 5.1.4). Subtract one for an informational rule (severity 1), whose evidence is weak. Force the confidence to 1 when the maintenance calendar or the allow-list explains the alert (Table 5.2-3).


Priority = impact × confidence, a score from 1 to 25, read on the matrix of Figure 5.2-B and converted into four bands with a time target each (Table 5.2-4): P1 Critical (16–25: acknowledge within fifteen minutes, open the incident record, call the owner and the contractor), P2 High (10–15: investigate today), P3 Medium (5–9: investigate this week, Monday review), P4 Low (1–4: monitor, close if nothing new in seven days). Two refinements are applied by hand after the score: an activity that is still going on moves up one band, and an alert about the health of the monitoring itself (a full log disk, a silent log source) is never ranked below P2, because while it lasts every other detection is a potential false negative.


Why multiply rather than add? Because a certain alert about a trivial asset (impact 1, confidence 5) and an uncertain alert about a critical asset (impact 5, confidence 1) should both rank low, while only the alert that is both serious and credible should reach the top; a product does that, a sum does not.




5.2.6 Aggregation, correlation and the known-good lists


Three mechanical operations make a queue readable. Aggregation merges records of the same kind into one alert: the 23 SSH (Secure Shell) failures are one alert with a count of 23, not 23 alerts; most tools do this by grouping on rule, asset and source address within a window (sixty minutes is common). Correlation links different alerts that share an entity — the same host, account or address — and is the basis of the corroboration bonus: alerts A-02, A-03 and A-08 all concern WS-10-44 and together describe one story (a scan, an outbound contact on port 4444, a query to a domain registered eleven days ago) that no single alert tells. The known-good lists remove what is already explained: the allow-list (addresses, accounts and behaviour patterns documented as legitimate, with the reason and the document that proves it) and the maintenance calendar (planned windows with the asset, the activity and the responsible person).


One pitfall deserves its own paragraph because Example 5.2 was built around it. A maintenance window is matched on asset, time and activity. The nightly backup window of SRV-AD01 runs from 02:00 to 03:00 and explains the batch logon of backup-svc at 02:00 (alert A-04). If the window were matched on asset and time alone, alert A-05 — fifteen failures on "administrator" at 02:40 from an unknown VPN (Virtual Private Network) address — would also fall inside it and be closed as expected activity. Attackers do not consult your calendar, but they do like quiet hours; a known-good rule that is too broad is a false negative waiting to happen.




5.2.7 Recording the decision


A triage decision that is not written down does not exist: on Monday nobody can tell whether A-09 was examined or forgotten. The minimal record — a ticket, a row in a spreadsheet, a note in the monitoring tool — contains the fields of Table 5.2-5: alert identifier; time in UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) and local time; source and rule; asset, account and addresses; category and outcome; impact, confidence and priority with their justification; the decision and the next step with a name and a date; pointers to the evidence (the raw log lines, the file names, the packet capture) rather than copies of it; and the status. Two disciplines go with the record. Evidence is preserved, never edited: you copy the raw lines, you do not "clean" them, and you record the time at which you looked. And monitoring data is confidential: the records contain who logged on, when, from where, and what they did; sections 6.7, 7.2 and 17 of the Cyber.SoHo Legal Notice, and the privacy obligations summarised in its section 8.3, apply to every ticket you write, including in Lab 3.




5.2.8 Alert fatigue and the six common mistakes


Alert fatigue is the state of a person or a team that receives more alerts than it can read with attention; the predictable result is that alerts are closed without being examined, and the real incident is closed with them. The cure is upstream (fewer, better alerts — Topic 6) and downstream (the triage discipline of this lesson). The six mistakes that produce it, in the order in which beginners make them:


    

  1. Ordering the queue by rule severity alone. Severity ignores the asset and the context; priority does not.
    2. 

  2. Handling the newest alert first. The queue is ordered by priority, then by age: the oldest alert of a band goes first.
    3. 

  3. Closing without a reason. Every closure names the calendar entry, the allow-list line or the rule defect. "Looks fine" is not a reason.
    4. 

  4. Ignoring health alerts. A full log disk (A-01) or a silent log source (A-12) is a loss of visibility; while it lasts, the quiet queue proves nothing.
    5. 

  5. Treating a quiet queue as a safe network. Silence is also what a false negative looks like; the only remedy is coverage (Topic 6.3) and periodic review of the baseline.
    6. 

  6. Over-broad known-good rules. The maintenance-window pitfall of 5.2.6: every exception must name the activity it excuses.
    7. 



With these in place the technician of Atelier Nordik can process the Saturday queue in under an hour, and the output — an ordered queue with a reason on every line — is exactly what the analysis of lesson 5.3 begins with on Thursday.

Example 5.2 — Saturday 14:00: twelve alerts in the weekend queue
Task of the example. Triage the twelve alerts that accumulated on MON-250 between Friday 18:00 and Saturday 13:00: remove the ones explained by the maintenance calendar and the allow-list, score the impact and the confidence of the others, compute the priority, assign a decision to each, and produce the ordered queue with a written reason on every line.


Relation to the lesson. The example performs the three verbs of 5.2.2 on real-looking alerts, uses the five questions of 5.2.3 to fill the two scales of 5.2.5, applies the aggregation and known-good mechanics of 5.2.6 (including the maintenance-window pitfall), and records the decisions in the form required by 5.2.7.


Lab 3 deliverable. The output file triage_queue.csv is the "sort" deliverable of Lab 3 and the starting point of its "diagnose" part; the alerts, the asset inventory, the allow-list and the maintenance calendar are the files you will reuse.
The twelve alerts are listed in Table 5.2-6. Four of them you already know from Class 14, now repeated on the second weekend: the port-scan pattern from WS-10-44 towards srv-web01 (A-02, sixteen ports in forty-two seconds, second occurrence), the six unanswered SYN (synchronize flag of a TCP segment) packets from WS-10-44 to 198.51.100.200 on port 4444 (A-03), the fifteen failures on "administrator" from the VPN (Virtual Private Network) address 10.8.0.9 (A-05) and the twenty-three SSH (Secure Shell) failures from 203.0.113.57 on srv-web01 (A-06). The others are new: the log disk of MON-250 at 86 % (A-01), the batch logon of backup-svc at 02:00 (A-04), a clock drift of 2.4 seconds on WS-10-31 (A-07), a DNS (Domain Name System) query from WS-10-44 to a domain registered eleven days ago (A-08), antivirus definitions that failed to update on three workstations (A-09), three failed logons followed by a success for ldube from her documented VPN (Virtual Private Network) address (A-10), a 1.2 GB download from the vendor update mirror to SRV-AD01 (A-11) and — last to arrive — srv-web01 silent since 11:20, no syslog received for more than an hour (A-12).


Run alert_triage.py. Pass 1 finds three explained alerts: A-04 (backup window, account backup-svc), A-10 (the allow-listed VPN (Virtual Private Network) address of ldube, and the documented "three failures then success" pattern) and A-11 (the vendor synchronisation window with the allow-listed mirror address). Pass 2 scores the nine others. The top of the queue holds four P1 items: A-02 (impact 4: rule severity 4 on a criticality-2 workstation; confidence 5: an unexplained destination plus two other alerts on the same host), A-05 (impact 5: domain controller and privileged account; confidence 4: unknown VPN (Virtual Private Network) address, no corroboration), A-06 (impact 4; confidence 5: Internet source, corroborated by A-12 on the same server) and A-12 (impact 4; confidence 4: the server under attack has gone silent). Then come A-03 and A-08 (P2, the two other pieces of the WS-10-44 story), A-01 (P2, the health of the monitoring), A-09 (P3) and A-07 (P4). The three explained alerts close at the bottom with their reasons.


Read the queue as a story rather than a list: a workstation is probing the web server and trying to reach the outside on port 4444; somebody is guessing the administrator password through the VPN (Virtual Private Network); somebody on the Internet is guessing SSH (Secure Shell) passwords on the web server, and that server has now stopped sending logs; and the monitoring server itself is running out of disk. Four incidents' worth of questions — and the answers are the work of lesson 5.3 and Lab 3.
The code that illustrates the example — alert_triage.py
What the script does. alert_triage.py reads the four input files (alerts_weekend.csv, assets.csv, allowlist.csv, maintenance_calendar.csv), finds the alerts explained by planned work or documented known-good behaviour (pass 1), scores impact and confidence for the others (pass 2), computes the priority, assigns a band and a decision, sorts the queue and writes triage_queue.csv.


Relation to the lecture. in_maintenance() and in_allowlist() are the known-good lists of 5.2.6 (with the asset-time-activity match that avoids the pitfall); impact_score() and confidence_score() are the two scales of 5.2.5; BANDS and band_for() are the priority bands and decisions; the output columns are the ticket fields of 5.2.7. The simulator below runs the same steps in the page, alert by alert, and places each alert on the priority matrix as it is scored.
alert_triage.py — a comment line before every line of code
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# ============================================================================
# alert_triage.py — Class 15, Example 5.2 (Atelier Nordik inc., fictional)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# TASK: take the alerts that accumulated in the monitoring queue over the
# weekend (alerts_weekend.csv), remove the ones explained by the allow-list or
# the maintenance calendar, estimate for each remaining alert its IMPACT (how
# bad if true) and its CONFIDENCE (how likely to be true), combine them into a
# PRIORITY score, assign a decision (escalate / investigate today / this week /
# monitor / close as benign) and write the ordered triage queue
# (triage_queue.csv). That queue is the starting point of the "diagnose and
# report" part of Lab 3.
# RELATION TO THE LECTURE: lesson 5.2 teaches that triage = categorise +
# prioritise + decide, and that priority is impact combined with likelihood
# (confidence), never the raw rule severity alone. This script is that method
# written as code, step by step.
# Educational material — Cyber.SoHo / Asen Grozdanov — (c) 2026 Cyber.SoHo.
# Use only in an authorized lab environment (Legal Notice v2.0, section 7.2).

# The csv module reads the four input files and writes the output queue.
import csv
# The datetime module parses alert times and maintenance windows so they can be compared.
from datetime import datetime

# Input: the alerts produced by the monitoring server between Friday 18:00 and Saturday 13:00.
ALERTS_FILE = "alerts_weekend.csv"
# Input: the asset inventory of Lab 1 with a criticality value (1 = low ... 5 = critical).
ASSETS_FILE = "assets.csv"
# Input: known-good addresses, accounts and patterns documented during Lab 2.
ALLOWLIST_FILE = "allowlist.csv"
# Input: the planned maintenance windows (backup, patching, synchronisation).
MAINTENANCE_FILE = "maintenance_calendar.csv"
# Output: the ordered queue with impact, confidence, priority, band, decision and reason.
OUTPUT_FILE = "triage_queue.csv"
# Accounts that hold elevated rights; an alert on them raises the impact by one level.
PRIVILEGED = {"administrator", "ops", "backup-svc"}
# Priority bands: lowest score of each band, its label and the decision that goes with it.
BANDS = [(16, "P1 Critical", "Escalate now: open an incident record and call the asset owner"),
         (10, "P2 High", "Investigate today (Topic 5.3 analysis steps)"),
         (5, "P3 Medium", "Investigate this week; add to the Monday review"),
         (0, "P4 Low", "Monitor; close if nothing new within 7 days")]


# Generic helper: read a CSV file and return a list of row dictionaries.
def read_rows(path):
    # Open the file in text mode with the newline setting recommended for CSV.
    with open(path, newline="") as f:
        # Materialise the reader into a list so the file can be closed immediately.
        return list(csv.DictReader(f))


# Helper: parse "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM" into a datetime object.
def parse_time(text):
    # strptime builds the datetime from the text using the given format.
    return datetime.strptime(text, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M")


# Step 1 — Is the alert explained by a maintenance window on the same asset?
def in_maintenance(alert, windows):
    # Convert the alert time once.
    when = parse_time(alert["time"])
    # Look at every planned window.
    for w in windows:
        # The window must concern the same asset (or the generic workstation pool).
        same_asset = w["asset"] == alert["asset"]
        # The alert time must fall inside the window (start included, end excluded).
        inside = parse_time(w["start"]) <= when < parse_time(w["end"])
        # The window must also describe the SAME activity: its scope is "*" (any), the account of the alert, or an address in the alert.
        same_activity = w["scope"] == "*" or w["scope"] == alert["account"] or w["scope"] in alert["address"]
        # Only when asset, time AND activity match is the alert explained by planned work (time alone is never enough).
        if same_asset and inside and same_activity:
            # Return the description of the window as the reason.
            return w["description"]
    # No window matched: return None, which Python treats as "false".
    return None


# Step 2 — Is the alert explained by the allow-list (known-good address, account or pattern)?
def in_allowlist(alert, allow):
    # Examine every allow-list entry.
    for a in allow:
        # Network entries match when the address text of the alert contains the allowed address.
        if a["kind"] == "network" and a["value"] in alert["address"]:
            # Return the documented reason.
            return a["reason"]
        # Account entries match when the account of the alert is the allowed account.
        if a["kind"] == "account" and a["value"] == alert["account"]:
            # Return the documented reason.
            return a["reason"]
        # Pattern entries match a specific, documented benign behaviour described in the rule name.
        if a["kind"] == "pattern" and a["value"] == "failed-logon<=3-then-success" and "followed by success" in alert["rule"]:
            # Return the documented reason.
            return a["reason"]
    # Nothing matched.
    return None


# Step 3 — Impact (1-5): how bad would it be if the alert is true?
def impact_score(alert, criticality):
    # Start from the larger of the rule severity and the criticality of the asset concerned.
    score = max(int(alert["rule_severity"]), criticality)
    # A privileged account raises the stakes by one level.
    if alert["account"] in PRIVILEGED:
        # Add one level.
        score += 1
    # Never exceed 5.
    return min(score, 5)


# Step 4 — Confidence (1-5): how likely is it that the alert describes real unwanted activity?
# "all_alerts" must contain only the alerts that are NOT already explained (benign alerts never corroborate).
def confidence_score(alert, all_alerts, allow):
    # Every alert starts at 3: "plausible, unverified".
    score = 3
    # Build the set of allowed network addresses to test the source/destination of the alert.
    allowed_addresses = [a["value"] for a in allow if a["kind"] == "network"]
    # An address that is neither local, nor empty, nor allow-listed makes the alert more credible.
    external = alert["address"] not in ("-", "local") and not any(v in alert["address"] for v in allowed_addresses)
    # Add one level for an unexplained external or unknown address.
    if external:
        # Raise the score.
        score += 1
    # Corroboration: another alert about the same asset in the queue makes both more credible.
    others = [b for b in all_alerts if b["alert_id"] != alert["alert_id"] and b["asset"] == alert["asset"]]
    # Add one level when at least one other alert concerns the same asset.
    if others:
        # Raise the score.
        score += 1
    # Informational rules (severity 1) are weak evidence: lower the confidence by one level.
    if int(alert["rule_severity"]) <= 1:
        # Lower the score.
        score -= 1
    # Keep the result inside 1-5.
    return max(1, min(score, 5))


# Step 5 — Convert the priority score into a band and a decision.
def band_for(score):
    # Bands are listed from the highest minimum to the lowest.
    for minimum, label, decision in BANDS:
        # The first band whose minimum is reached is the right one.
        if score >= minimum:
            # Return the label and the decision text.
            return label, decision
    # Defensive default (should never be reached because the last minimum is 0).
    return "P4 Low", BANDS[-1][2]


# Main routine: read, triage, sort, write, print.
def main():
    # Read the alerts.
    alerts = read_rows(ALERTS_FILE)
    # Read the asset inventory and index it by asset name for quick lookup.
    assets = {a["asset"]: a for a in read_rows(ASSETS_FILE)}
    # Read the allow-list.
    allow = read_rows(ALLOWLIST_FILE)
    # Read the maintenance calendar.
    windows = read_rows(MAINTENANCE_FILE)
    # Prepare the list of triaged results.
    queue = []
    # Pass 1 — find the alerts explained by planned work or documented known-good behaviour.
    explained = {}
    # Examine every alert.
    for alert in alerts:
        # Test the maintenance calendar first (planned work explains the alert).
        reason = in_maintenance(alert, windows)
        # Then test the allow-list (documented known-good behaviour).
        if reason is None:
            # Only test the allow-list when no maintenance window matched.
            reason = in_allowlist(alert, allow)
        # Remember the reason (or None) for this alert id.
        explained[alert["alert_id"]] = reason
    # The alerts that remain unexplained are the only ones allowed to corroborate each other.
    open_alerts = [a for a in alerts if explained[a["alert_id"]] is None]
    # Pass 2 — score every alert in the order it arrived.
    for alert in alerts:
        # Look up the criticality of the asset (2 = generic workstation when unknown).
        criticality = int(assets.get(alert["asset"], {"criticality": "2"})["criticality"])
        # Compute the impact.
        impact = impact_score(alert, criticality)
        # Fetch the explanation found in pass 1.
        reason = explained[alert["alert_id"]]
        # Expected activity is a "benign true positive": the rule fired correctly on authorised activity.
        if reason:
            # Confidence that something unwanted happened is minimal.
            confidence = 1
            # The priority score is still computed for the record.
            score = impact * confidence
            # The band is informational.
            band = "Benign (expected)"
            # The decision is to close with the documented reason.
            decision = "Close as expected activity; keep the record"
        # Otherwise estimate the confidence and derive the band from the score.
        else:
            # Estimate the likelihood that the alert is real (only unexplained alerts can corroborate).
            confidence = confidence_score(alert, open_alerts, allow)
            # Priority = impact x confidence (1..25).
            score = impact * confidence
            # Convert the score into a band and a decision.
            band, decision = band_for(score)
            # Build the reason text from the factors that were used.
            reason = f"impact {impact} (rule {alert['rule_severity']}, asset {criticality}) x confidence {confidence}"
        # Store the triaged alert.
        queue.append({"alert_id": alert["alert_id"], "time": alert["time"], "asset": alert["asset"],
                      "rule": alert["rule"], "impact": impact, "confidence": confidence,
                      "priority_score": score, "band": band, "decision": decision, "reason": reason})
    # Sort: open alerts before benign ones, then highest score first, then earliest time first.
    queue.sort(key=lambda r: (r["band"].startswith("Benign"), -r["priority_score"], r["time"]))
    # Add the position in the queue (1 = handle first).
    for position, row in enumerate(queue, start=1):
        # Insert the position as the first column.
        row["queue_position"] = position
    # Write the queue to the output file.
    with open(OUTPUT_FILE, "w", newline="") as f:
        # Put queue_position first, then the other columns.
        fieldnames = ["queue_position"] + [k for k in queue[0].keys() if k != "queue_position"]
        # Create the writer.
        writer = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=fieldnames)
        # Write the header.
        writer.writeheader()
        # Write all rows.
        writer.writerows(queue)
    # Print the queue so the technician sees the order immediately.
    print(f"Triaged {len(queue)} alerts -> {OUTPUT_FILE}")
    # One line per alert: position, id, score, band and a short reason.
    for r in queue:
        # Aligned columns for readability on the screen.
        print(f"  #{r['queue_position']:<2} {r['alert_id']}  score={r['priority_score']:>2}  {r['band']:<18} {r['asset']:<10} {r['decision']}")


# Run main() only when the script is executed directly.
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Start the program.
    main()

Execution log (every step; pause to discuss)
Step-by-step explanation of the script
  1. Constants. The four input file names, the output name, the set of privileged accounts, and the BANDS table (minimum score, label, decision) — the policy of 5.2.5 written once, at the top, where it can be changed.
  2. Helpers. read_rows() loads a CSV (Comma-Separated Values) file as a list of dictionaries; parse_time() converts "2026-10-10 02:40" into a comparable date object.
  3. Known-good checks. in_maintenance() returns the description of a window only when the asset, the time and the activity (the scope column: an account, an address or "*") match. in_allowlist() returns the documented reason when a network address, an account or a named pattern matches.
  4. Impact. impact_score() takes the larger of the rule severity and the asset criticality, adds one for a privileged account, and caps the result at 5.
  5. Confidence. confidence_score() starts at 3, adds one for an unexplained external address, adds one when another open alert concerns the same asset, subtracts one for an informational rule, and keeps the result between 1 and 5. Benign alerts are excluded from the corroboration test, so that three expected alerts on SRV-AD01 do not inflate the confidence of a fourth.
  6. Pass 1 and pass 2. main() first finds the explained alerts, then scores every alert: explained alerts receive confidence 1 and the band "Benign (expected)"; the others receive impact × confidence, a band and a decision from band_for(), and a reason that lists the factors.
  7. Sorting and output. Open alerts before benign ones, highest score first, oldest first at equal score; a queue position is added and the result is written to triage_queue.csv and printed. Run it with python3 alert_triage.py in the folder that contains the four input files.

Flash cards — lesson 5.2
Click a card to reveal the answer on its back; click again to return.
Card 1
What are the three verbs of triage, according to the FIRST (Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams) CSIRT (Computer Security Incident Response Team) Services Framework?
click to reveal
Answer 1
Categorise (what kind of alert and what outcome), prioritise (impact × confidence) and produce an initial assessment — in this course: decide and record.
Card 2
Severity versus priority — what is the difference?
click to reveal
Answer 2
Severity is the value attached to the rule by its author, before any context. Priority is computed during triage from the impact on this asset and the confidence that the alert is real; it decides the order of work.
Card 3
How is the confidence score built in Example 5.2?
click to reveal
Answer 3
Start at 3; +1 for an unexplained external address; +1 when another open alert concerns the same asset (corroboration); −1 for an informational rule; forced to 1 when the calendar or the allow-list explains the alert.
Card 4
Why must a maintenance window be matched on asset, time AND activity?
click to reveal
Answer 4
Because an attacker can act during a quiet window: matched on asset and time only, the 02:00–03:00 backup window would have closed the administrator-guessing burst of 02:40 as expected activity.
Card 5
Which two alerts are never ranked below P2, whatever their score, and why?
click to reveal
Answer 5
Health alerts about the monitoring itself — a full log disk, a silent log source — because while they last every other detection is a potential false negative.
Check-in questions — lesson 5.2
Four multiple-choice questions (one answer each) and two multiple-select questions (the number of expected answers is written in round brackets). Use Hint for a clue, Check to grade your selection, Reveal to see the expected answer and the explanation of every option.
MCQ (Multiple-Choice Question)Question 1


An alert has rule severity 2 ("disk usage ≥ 85 %") on MON-250, the monitoring server (criticality 4). No account, no external address, no other alert on the asset. Using the scales of Example 5.2, what are its impact, confidence and priority?
  • Wrong: the impact is the larger of 2 and 4, not the rule severity alone.
  • Correct: impact max(2, 4) = 4; confidence 3 (no bonus, no malus); 4 × 3 = 12, band P2 — and the health rule of 5.2.5 keeps it at P2 at least.
  • Wrong: there is no external address and no corroboration, so the confidence stays at 3.
  • Wrong: confidence 1 is reserved for alerts explained by the calendar or the allow-list.
Hint: Impact takes the larger of rule severity and asset criticality; confidence starts at 3 and nothing adds or subtracts.


MCQ (Multiple-Choice Question)Question 2


Why does alert A-05 (15 failures on "administrator" from 10.8.0.9 at 02:40) NOT get closed by the 02:00–03:00 backup window of SRV-AD01?
  • Wrong: both are on Saturday October 10; the time does fall inside the window.
  • Wrong: A-05 is on SRV-AD01, the same asset as the window; asset and time match — that is exactly the danger.
  • Correct: the window's scope is the backup-svc account; the activity of A-05 (administrator, failed logons) is not the one the window excuses.
  • Wrong: every alert is tested against the calendar; what protects A-05 is the activity match, not its severity.
Hint: Reread the pitfall of 5.2.6: asset, time and activity.


MCQ (Multiple-Choice Question)Question 3


Which outcome category should the technician write for alert A-11 (1.2 GB downloaded from the allow-listed vendor mirror 203.0.113.80 during the synchronisation window)?
  • Wrong: the rule worked exactly as written; nothing is broken in it.
  • Correct: the transfer really happened and is authorised and documented (contract, window, allow-list); close with the reference and consider a tuning exception in Topic 6.
  • Wrong: the activity is authorised; it is not unwanted.
  • Wrong: no other open alert describes the same cause.
Hint: Did the rule work correctly? Was the activity real and authorised?


MCQ (Multiple-Choice Question)Question 4


Two alerts have the same priority score of 20: A-02 (Friday 19:12) and A-06 (Saturday 03:14). In which order does the queue list them, and why?
  • Wrong: the source of an alert enters the confidence score, not the tie-break; the technician may still move it up with a written reason.
  • Correct: priority first, then age — the oldest alert of a band is handled first.
  • Wrong: handling the newest first is one of the six common mistakes.
  • Wrong: no tie-break uses the asset name.
Hint: Mistake number 2 of 5.2.8.


MSQ (Multiple-Select Question)Question 5


Which fields belong in the minimal triage record of an alert? (select 4)
  • Correct: identification of the alert.
  • Correct: the assessment, with the reasons that produced it.
  • Wrong: evidence is preserved, never "cleaned"; a modified record is worthless in an investigation.
  • Correct: the decision and who does what by when.
  • Correct: pointers to the raw evidence, unmodified.
  • Wrong: monitoring records are confidential and factual; opinions about people have no place in them.
Hint: Table 5.2-5: identification, assessment, decision, evidence — and two disciplines: never edit evidence, keep data confidential.


MSQ (Multiple-Select Question)Question 6


Which of the following raise the confidence that an alert is real, according to the method of this lesson? (select 3)
  • Correct: corroboration adds one level.
  • Correct: an unexplained external party adds one level.
  • Wrong: an informational rule is weak evidence and lowers the confidence by one.
  • Correct: recurrence of an unexplained pattern makes it more credible, not less (5.2.4, duplicates).
  • Wrong: a matching window explains the alert and forces the confidence to 1.
  • Wrong: the criticality of the asset raises the impact, not the confidence.
Hint: Confidence is about likelihood of being real; impact is about how bad. Separate the two.

  • Cyber.SoHo — Legal Notice, Terms of Use and Acceptable Use Policy (v2.0)

    The reference publication for incident handling, now organised around the NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) CSF (Cybersecurity Framework) 2.0 functions. Its "Detect" and "Respond" material is where analysis and prioritisation of events sit.
  • NIST SP 800-94 — Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDPS)
    Defines signature-based, anomaly-based and stateful protocol analysis detection, and the terms false positive and false negative, exactly as used in lesson 5.1.
  • NIST SP 800-92 — Guide to Computer Security Log Management
    The log-management guide behind Topic 4: generation, storage, analysis and the review process that feeds triage.
  • NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0
    The six functions Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover. "Detect" (continuous monitoring, adverse event analysis) is the frame of this whole course.
  • Canadian Centre for Cyber Security — Developing your incident response plan (ITSAP.40.003)
    Canadian federal guidance: preparation, detection and analysis, containment, eradication, recovery, lessons learned. Written for small and medium organisations such as Atelier Nordik.

    Alerts, advisories and baseline controls for Canadian organisations; the first public source to consult when an indicator looks like a known campaign.

    Video used in lesson 5.2 (9:14): the incident response process in which triage is the first analysis step.
  • MyDFIR — SOC Alert Triage Explained: What Most Beginners Get Wrong
    Optional video for lesson 5.2 from a practitioner channel: the thinking of an analyst in front of an alert queue. Reachable on the day of writing; its length is not published on any page the author could read, so watch the first fifteen minutes.
  • OPNsense — official site
    The firewall of the Atelier Nordik network; its logs produce alerts A-02, A-03 and A-11.
  • Wazuh — official site
    Open-source security monitoring platform of the kind installed on MON-250 in Lab 2 (log collection, rules, alerts).
  • Suricata — official site
    Open-source IDS (Intrusion Detection System) / IPS (Intrusion Prevention System): an example of signature-based and anomaly-based network detection discussed in 5.1.4.
  • Wireshark — official site
    The packet analyser of Class 14; still the tool to confirm what an alert claims about the traffic.
  • Dawson College — Institutional Student Evaluation Policy (ISEP)
    Rules for quizzes, labs and exams, including academic integrity; Quiz 3 is run under this policy.
  • BAnQ — free online account
    Required reading access (O'Reilly, LinkedIn Learning) listed in the course outline.
